newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Hutu refugees resettle after attack on Zaire camp.
newsitem.headline: Hutu refugees resettle after attack on Zaire camp.

text.p: Nearly 20,000 Hutus who fled their refugee camp in eastern Zaire after it was attacked by ethnic Tutsis have resettled in nearby camps, aid sources said on Monday.

"Runingo camp is almost empty with only a few hundred refugees left. The others have reached other camps and are trying to stay with friends or relatives," a foreign aid worker, in touch with Zaire from neighbouring Burundi, told Reuters.
The U.N. refugee agency, UNHCR, says four Hutu refugees were killed in the raid on Runingo early on Sunday.

It was the first such attack on any of the 12 camps in Zaire's South Kivu province where 230,000 Hutus from Burundi and Rwanda live. About one million Hutu refugees are in eastern Zaire's two provinces and are perceived as a permanent threat to the minority Tutsis who control the armies of both Rwanda and Burundi.
Both countries say the camps are bases for Hutu rebel infiltrators.
Rwanda has told the men among the 300-400,000 Banyamulenge, who moved to what is now Zaire as long as 200 years ago, to stand and resist a campaign to expel them.
There is growing evidence that Rwanda and to a lesser extent Burundi are assisting the Banyamulenge, diplomatic sources say.
Reasons include ethnic ties and the advantage of having an allied force in eastern Zaire to make life much harder for the Hutu rebels based there.
The aid sources did not want to be quoted by name but were in little doubt that Sunday's assailants were Banyamulenge, ready to fight Zairean troops.
"They could have killed hundreds of refugees in Runingo if they had wanted to but all they did was shoot up nine tents," a senior aid official told Reuters.
Humanitarian sources in Zaire's capital Kinshasa reported up to 100 Banyamulenge fighters, with small arms and mortars, reaching Runingo from the Burundian border a few kilometres away.
"It looks like their mission was to close the camp so that their cross-border movements are not seen and they are not counted," the aid official said.

Burundi's army spokesman, Lieutenant-Colonel Isaie Nibizi, told Reuters last week it was untrue Burundi was helping the Banyamulenge fighters by allowing them to cross into Zaire after training in Rwanda.
UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg said at the last tally on September 6 there were 19,000 Hutu refugees in Runingo, 11,000 Burundians and 8,000 Rwandans.
The Burundians started arriving in 1993 during ethnic clashes and the Rwandans fled in 1994 after hardline Hutus killed up to one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

Zairean troops, apparently incensed by casualties fighting the guerrillas, went on a looting spree last week in Uvira, the lakeside town on the other side of the border from Burundi's capital, Bujumbura.

United Nations and private relief organisations, who manage the refugee camps among other tasks, have steadily withdrawn foreign staff from Uvira in the past week. Nine more were evacuated by air to Kenya on Sunday, including four UNHCR staff, U.N. sources said.
